title: The Magic Lamp of Fatehpur Sikri (KN)
summary: A merchant sells an 'Aladdin's lamp' to a gullible prince. Birbal demonstrates that real genies are summoned through human sweat.
full_text:
A foreign trickster arrived at the court of Prince Salim (the future Emperor Jahangir), carrying an antique, tarnished brass oil lamp covered in mysterious Arabic inscriptions. The trickster whispered secretly to the young prince:

'Your Highness! This is an authentic magic lamp from the cavern of Baghdad! If you rub the brass with saffron oil at midnight, a giant celestial genie will emerge to build golden palaces and defeat your enemies in battle! I offer it to you for merely ten thousand gold mohurs!'

Salim was fascinated and paid the ten thousand gold coins from his royal allowance.

For seven nights, the young prince rubbed the lamp with scented oil, chanted spells, and waited in the dark, but nothing emerged except greasy brass soot!

Realizing he had been swindled, Salim was furious and complained to his father, Emperor Akbar.

Akbar summoned Birbal to track down the swindler.

Birbal caught the trickster at the city gates, retrieved the prince's gold, and brought the lamp into the council chamber.

Young Prince Salim asked: 'Raja Birbal, is there truly no magic lamp in the world that commands a genie?'

Birbal picked up the brass lamp, handed Salim an iron spade and a book of mathematics, and said with affectionate warmth:

'My Prince, there is indeed a magic lamp that commands the greatest genie in creation, but it is not made of brass.

'The magic lamp is the Human Intellect!

'The oil that fuels it is Diligent Study and Truth!

'The flame that burns upon it is Moral Virtue!

'And the mighty genie that emerges from it to build golden cities, drain swamps, heal diseases, and conquer empires is the genie of Honest Human Labor and Science!

'He who rubs the lamp of his own mind with hard work and study can command the universe. But he who sits in the dark rubbing a metal pot, waiting for magic to do his work, is a fool who loses his gold to swindlers!'

Prince Salim bowed in deep respect, took the lesson to heart, and dedicated himself to his studies, while Akbar praised Birbal's inspiring pedagogy.
